subtopic: DISPATCH FROM COLONIAL SECRETARY REFERRED TO IN DEBATE ON A CANADIAN FLAG

speechtext: On the order for motions:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DISPATCH FROM COLONIAL SECRETARY REFERRED TO IN DEBATE ON A CANADIAN FLAG
speechtext:
Yesterday the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) asked if I would lay on the table the dispatch from Colonial Secretary Harcourt concerning the flag that is flown in Canada, to which reference had been made on the previous evening. I have the dispatch in my hand and I think it would be of interest to hon. members generally to be apprised of it. If the house will permit, I should like to read the communications. The first is:
Ebenezer, Saskatchewan, Canada, March 11, 1911.
The Secretary,
His Imperial Majesty,
King George V.
My Lord,
I am the teacher at one of the public schools in the Canadian northwest.
An order has recently been issued by the department of education that every school in the dominion shall fly the national flag, and there seems some uncertainty amongst the people in this locality as to the flag this school shall have. I hold that the Union Jack pure and simple, is the national flag of the British empire throughout the world; but find some people on this side of the Atlantic have a notion that the "red ensign" with Canadian coat of arms (the naval flag) should be used in Canada.
IMr. Howe.3
I shall be much obliged therefore if you would say which is in order.
Trusting to receive the favour of your reply. I beg, etc.,
John F. Stedman.
Colonial Secretary Harcourt wrote to the Governor General in connection with this letter as follows:
Downing Street,
12 April, 1911.
My Lord,
I have the honour to transmit to Your Excellency a copy of a letter received by the King's private secretary from Mr. J. F. Stedman respecting the national flag to be flown in Canada.
I shall be glad if Your Excellency will cause the writer to be informed that the Union Jack is the national flag of Canada as of all other parts of His Majesty's dominions.
I have the honour to be,
My Lord,
Your Lordship's most obedient, humble servant,
L. Harcourt.
Governor General,
His Excellency,
The Right Honourable,
Earl Grey, G.C.M.G., G.C.Y.O.,
&c. &c.
There are two other communications I should like to read, the first being:
Ottawa, Ontario,
2nd May, 1912.
The Secretary of State for the Colonies,
London.
Dear Sir,
Will you kindly inform me what is, according to correct usage, the proper flag for a citizen of the British empire to use in his own grounds or on his house on say 24th May or Dominion day or other occasion when flags are used.
I mean by this, is the red ensign correct on land: as it is said by some to be the exclusive flag of the merchant marine. Is the flag of Canada correct for this decorative purpose? (Red ensign with badge of Canada in the fly.) Is the Union Jack correct? May any or all of these flags be used by a private citizen, who has no official rank?
Kindly address me, care of the general office: National Transcontinental railway, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada.
Yours very truly,
George S. Hodgins.
The next communication, reads:
Downing Street,
21st May, 1912.
Sir:
I have the honour to transmit to your Royal Highness a copy of a letter from Mr. G. S. Hodgins in regard to the flag which should be used by private persons who are British subjects.

Questions
2.	I should be glad if you would be good enough to cause Mr. Hodgins to be informed that the Union flag is the national flag of Canada as of all other parts of His Majesty's dominions, and may be flown on land by all British subjects: and that the red ensign, with the arms of the dominion of Canada in the fly, is intended to be used only by Canadian merchant vessels.
I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your Royal Highness' most obedient humble servant,
L. Harcourt.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: K.G., K.T., K.P., G.C.B., G.C.S.I., G.C.M.G., G.C.I.E., G.C.V.O.,
speechtext: It will be remembered that I directed the attention of the house to the fact that the colonial secretary did not of his own motion undertake to declare officially what was the Canadian flag. It will be recalled that I made that quite clear on the pages of Hansard. My argument has been abundantly verified; for it will be observed that Mr. Harcourt was simply answering a question which had been directed to His Majesty the King by a citizen in Saskatchewan. It would hardly be correct to say that that was the first official statement as to what the flag of Canada was; for there was a circular showing that the official flag of the whole British Empire was what was called the union jack, and it was not until long after that, that there was any question of any other flag being used by any part of the king's dominions. But the point I tried to make was that under no circumstances did the colonial secretary undertake to indicate what the position was except in answer to an inquiry directed to the king by the teacher in Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: K.G., K.T., K.P., G.C.B., G.C.S.I., G.C.M.G., G.C.I.E., G.C.V.O.,
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to discuss the matter, but what my right hon. friend has just stated makes it necessary for me to point out that what he has said is not entirely correct. It is correct with respect to one of the communications I read, but not with respect to the other. The second communication was from George S. Hodgins of Ottawa, addressed to the Secretary of State for the Colonies, London, not to the secretary of His Majesty at all, asking if he could be informed as to the correct usage in respect to the flag, and the secretary of state replied to the governor general-there was no reference to His Majesty or to His Majesty's secretary-that he would be glad if the governor general would cause Mr. Hodgins to be informed that the union flag was the national flag of Canada.

1.	Yes, both of them, with J. Louis Marchand, Esq., of Three Rivers, P.Q., as associate counsel, in cases instituted by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, in the circumstances set forth in No. 2.
2.	The actions concern persons involved in an organization which covered a large area in the province of Quebec for the purpose of transporting and distributing illicit alcohol.
To date, 43 charges have been preferred under the provisions of the criminal code for conspiracy to defraud the revenue.
Investigations by the R.C.M. Police prior to the preferring of charges covered a period of almost two years and Messrs. Gerard Fauteux, K.C., and Fernand Choquette, K.C., were the original appointees as counsel for the Crown to assist in segregating the evidence and preparing charges entered at Montreal, Quebec City and Three Rivers, P.Q.
In view of the importance of these cases and the long study which the two legal counsel gave them from their inception, it was essential that their services be retained to prosecute at the three points mentioned.

For a return showing, (a) complete details of that portion of the 1935-1936 wheat crop disposed of by the Canadian wheat board between July 31, 1936, and December 31, 1937; (b) complete details of the disposal by the Canadian wheat board of wheat acquired from the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited, from July 31, 1936, to December 31, 1937.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
I am sure that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) will believe me when I say that there is not the slightest intention of withholding from him or from other members of the house any information which can be obtained with a reasonable degree of expenditure of time. I communicated with the chief commissioner of the wheat board with regard to the question, and I have a telegram from him stating that the securing of this information-
... involves complete details of sales of approximately 84 million bushels comprising innumerable entries. Tabulation and typing this information is vast undertaking. Our staff working under pressure and will be for next two months preparing for distributing seed and feed grain and if details as requested require be furnished shall have to employ additional staff under supervision heads of departments who are at present busy other work. Cannot estimate how quickly information could be made available. Assure you board have no deside evade responsibility this matter but imperative present full staff must be employed seed and feed work as time before seedine limited.
Motions for Papers

I read that to indicate that it is a tremendous task to secure this information, and under the circumstances I suggest to my hon. friend that he might drop the question.
No.

I cannot see that there is too much detail involved in preparing an answer to this question. A report of the operations of the board in respect to the 1935 crop was issued by the chairman of the board on July 31, 1936. As I remember it, there were some three million and several thousand bushels remaining of the 1935 crop. As the minister has stated, the balance, making up eighty-five or eighty-six million bushels, was taken over from the old wheat board. What I should like to know, and what I think it is quite easy to procure, is the number of bushels, indicating the different grades, and the price at which it was disposed of, in order to find out what would be the balance -a report similar to that which was issued, as the minister knows, on July 31, 1936, to show the final disposition of the balance of the wheat. I do not believe that a report such as was issued on that date would entail very much difficulty. It is not a detailed statement with respect to every man or every firm that bought a bushel of wheat; it is with respect to the number of bushels, the price at which they were sold, and the amount received for the balance.

I can only take the motion in the terms in which it is expressed. If the hon. gentleman does not really desire complete details, I suggest that if he could frame a simpler motion which will not entail all the expenditure of time and money that the present motion calls for and will involve, he should do so, and withdraw the present motion and submit another one.

May I direct the attention of the minister to the fact that the statute creating the wheat board provides that this information shall be sent to the minister, and that it is not from Winnipeg that this is sought; it is the information given in the weekly reports which are sent in and signed by the auditors that should be brought down.
My right hon. friend surely does not mean to intimate that all details of the various sales of eighty-four million bushels of wheat come to the minister. They assuredly do not.
Not all the details.

That information is in the possession of the board at Winnipeg, and nowhere else, and the information must be

compiled by the board in Winnipeg. I am compelled to accept the word of the chairman who, I think, is perhaps more familiar with the work entailed than anyone else is, and I am accepting his word in that regard.
Would the minister read the telegram he sent to the chairman?
I did not send him a telegram. Just for the information of my suspicious friend-

Now, the hon. gentleman will withdraw that. There is no reason why he should be thus out of order. Strange as it may seem, he has no right under the rules to say that. I ask the simple question because the rules require that the letter sent should be read as well as the reply. You cannot take one side of it only; and I ask the minister what he asked the Winnipeg people.

For the satisfaction of my right hon. friend-and I did not anticipate he would couch his reply quite in the language or the tone in which he did-I may say that when the motion first appeared on the order paper I simply took the leaf out of the order paper, sent it to Mr. Mclvor for his comment and made no suggestion whatsoever. I say that in anticipation, perhaps, of something else that might be said.
No, I did not say "suggestion."
I did not indicate in the slightest degree to Mr. Mclvor what his answer should be. I will say that in any case. As a matter of fact, I might as well make a complete story of it.

Mr. Speaker, on a question of order, standing order 51 reads:
Notices of motion for the production of papers which the member asking for the same intends to move without discussion, shall be marked by him with an asterisk and shall be placed by the clerk on the order paper above "Notices of Motions," under the heading "Notices of Motions for the Production of Papers." All such notices when called shall be forthwith disposed of; but, if on any such motion a debate be desired, it shall be transferred by the clerk to the order of notices of motions.
We have been hearing a debate for ten minutes, and I suggest that this motion, if not disposed of immediately, should be transferred to notices of motions.
The right hon. minister is right, of course.

The point that has been raised is well taken. These notices of motions for production of papers are not debatable.

Motions for Papers

At the risk of offending against the rules, I merely wish to say that my proposal to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) was that perhaps he could frame his motion in a simpler way so that it could be accepted.
I am agreeable to having it transferred to notices of motions.

With regard to this motion, the objection seems to be that, as worded, its meaning is not quite clear to the chairman of the wheat board. He does not understand what is meant by the words "or interest," and I suggest to my hon. friend that he draft the motion in such a way as to make perfectly clear what information he desires to obtain.
I can do that right here; simply strike out those words. I just want to know what were the open trades.
That is quite satisfactory.
According to the rules, the hon. gentleman cannot have three notices of motion under his name, so that if the first one is transferred I do not think it is in order to transfer the other two.

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. ROSS (Moose Jaw) moved:
subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext:
That a special committee, the members thereof to be selected at a later date, be appointed to investigate:
(a)	The application of the Customs Tariff by the officers and clerks of the Department of National Revenue;
(b)	The collection of customs duties;
(c)	The practice now followed in applying the present law respecting drawbacks;
And that the said special committee have power to send for persons, papers and records, to examine witnesses under oath, and to report from time to time.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, speaking in this
house on February 3 I said that the people of this country were being regimented into
purchasing their supplies from certain people in the country and at prices fixed in accordance with the ideas of those people. I said that the taxing power of parliament had been turned over to privileged interests, and that prices were being artificially raised in this country in order that certain industries might be subsidized. The levying of taxation is a function of parliament. I say now that through successive changes in the Customs Act and the Customs Tariff the authority of parliament in tariff making has been delegated to a department of the government, and that through rules and regulations laid down by that department an importer of goods to-day cannot discover by reading the tariff act as passed by parliament what amount of duty will be charged upon his goods when they arrive at the border.
As a matter of fact the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), as an importer of goods into this country, would be unable to-day to recognize his own handiwork. An act is brought down in this house purporting to set the rates of duty upon articles imported. By the time the rules and regulations of the department are applied the amount of money collected upon those articles is at a rate entirely different from that set by parliament when the act was passed. I am not here criticizing the Department of National Revenue; I am stating that we in this parliament have delegated to a department of the government the tariff-making powers of the House of Commons, and that the passing of a budget now simply becomes a hollow mockery. No importer of goods can gain any idea, from the act that we pass, as to how much money he will have to pay upon the goods being imported. No member of the House of Commons, no ordinary citizen, can import goods and know what he will have to pay. Even the best customs brokers in this country from time to time have to amend their entries in order to comply with the rules and regulations of the Department of National Revenue.
I say, Mr. Speaker, it is high time we in this house, and more especially the members on this side of the house, looked thoroughly into this matter, so that parliament may again perform this important function in order that the importation of goods may not be unduly restricted and discouraged, which of necessity must engender ill-will towards Canada in the countries to which we export. We on this side of the house were elected on a policy of expanding trade, and in many regards this government is entitled to great credit for having followed that policy up to date. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley also has credit due him for his actions
The Customs Tariff

in this regard, but there is still a great deal of barbed wire to be cleared away before we shall be able to import goods freely.
The principle of protection in Canada has been furthered in many ways. I will set them out under headings.
1.	By the raising of the ad valorem and specific duties.
2.	By the expansion of the number of items in the customs tariff.
3.	By the fixing of values for duty purposes.
4.	By the fixing of value for duty purposes in combination with the application of the anti-dumping legislation covering imports that compete with goods made or produced in Canada.
5.	By the extended application of the dumping duty.
6.	By drawbacks.
Over a period of years, Mr. Speaker, the ad valorem tariff has been raised in this country, and of late a habit has grown up of adding to that a specific tariff which in many cases amounts to more than the ad valorem rate. To some people this may seem to be a painless method, or perhaps it is done only in order to fool the people, who are the voters. In 1903 there were 645 items in the tariff, of which 447 were dutiable and the remainder free. At the present time there are over fifteen hundred items in the customs tariff, some of which are again subdivided. It is sometimes difficult to raise or lower the tariff upon an item which includes many articles. It is much easier to deal with these things if the item is split in order that it may include, perhaps, only one article. Possibly this has been done in order to mete out tariff favours to some people.
Under heading No. 3, Mr. Speaker, the simplest method of raising the tariff is through the raising of the value for duty purposes. At times it is very difficult to get parliament to raise or lower a tariff, but when parliament has passed the Customs Tariff and parliament has given the Department of National Revenue authority under the Customs Tariff and the Customs Act to value for duty purposes, it is a very simple matter to raise the value placed upon the goods to be imported, and thereby raise the rate simply because there are no members there to protest; simply because the people of Canada generally do not know what is going on.
I intend to use a hundred dollars' worth of goods as an example to show the successive changes in the Customs Act and the Customs Tariff. I am assuming that the rate of tariff has not been changed since 1867 I do not 
intend to place on Hansard all the amendments to the Customs Tariff and the Customs Act, but I ask the minister to be good enough to place these upon the order paper so that we may all know exactly what changes have been made. In 1867, under the Customs Act, the provision which is now section 35 of the Customs Act read as follows:
In all cases where any duty is imposed on any goods imported into Canada ad valorem or according to the value of such goods, such value shall be understood to be the fair market value thereof in the principal markets of the country whence the same were exported directly to Canada.
These were the qualifying words in the section dealing with value for duty purposes. That was meant to be the export price of goods in the principal markets of the country of origin. A hundred dollars' worth of goods coming in at forty per cent duty would pay $40. In 1883 the Act was amended and the qualifying section then read:
The value for duty shall be the fair market value thereof when sold for home consumption in the principal markets of the country of origin.
The home consumption value might mean an addition of ten per cent. Therefore, our one hundred dollars' worth of goods would be increased by ten per cent for the home consumption price. The duty value would then be $110 and with a tariff rate of forty per cent, this would mean the payment of $44. The result would be 44 per cent instead of the forty per cent as passed by the House of Commons.
Three changes were made to this section in 1921. The first change was that the value for duty should be determined by the wholesale price in the country of origin. The second change was that in no case should it be less than the cost of production, plus a reasonable amount for profit, and, third, that the minister was to be the sole judge of what that reasonable amount would be. We now have our hundred dollars' worth of goods with an export price of $100, plus twenty per cent for wholesale price, totalling $120. There would then be a profit of ten per cent if the minister did not happen to be a Canadian manufacturer, or probably twenty per cent if he were. The value for duty would now be $144, which at forty per cent would mean a payment of $57.60 or 57i% per cent as against the forty per cent provided for by the House of Commons.
In 1922 the section was amended to introduce exchange rates, and the value for duty was computed and levied under regulations passed by the minister. The rates set by parliament were used only as figures in the determination

The Customs Tariff
of the value. On our hundred dollars' worth of goods the minister's value might be $150. At forty per cent there would be a payment of $60, or a rate of 60 per cent. In 1937 the minister still had the right to determine the value and our example would give the same results.
Section 36 must be read in conjunction with this last section, number 35. In 1907 section 36 set the discount rate for cash that an exporter might allow to an importer. In other words, if an exporter wanted to allow an importer five per cent for cash, the customs department said that that could not be done; that two and a half per cent was the limit that could be allowed in setting the value for duty purposes. In 1930 this section really came into play. Taken along with section 35 it meant that the value for duty of imported goods in no case should be lower than the price to wholesalers or jobbers in the country of origin; that in no case was the value to be lower than the cost of production plus a reasonable advance for selling costs and profit. The minister was to be the sole judge of what that advance should be, and his figures were to be final. This meant that the authority of parliament to set rates had been delegated to the officers of the department.
In 1934 parliament delegated to the governor in council other rights and placed more authority in the hands of the minister and the department. In 1936 this section was amended and the provision that the minister was to be the sole judge was dropped. However, the value for duty was determined by the selling price for home consumption plus a reasonable advance for selling costs and profit. One hundred dollars' worth of goods would have ten per cent added to cover selling costs and twenty per cent to cover profit. This would make the final valuation $132. A rate of forty per cent would mean a payment of $52.80 or 52-8/10ths per cent instead of the forty per cent set by parliament.
This is not all. Customs officials must now be able to determine the production costs in other countries and must be able to State what are reasonable selling costs and what would be a reasonable profit. This is in order that further protection may be given to Canadian manufacturers. The other day I heard a phrase used in this house which sticks in my memory. It was "compensatory adjustments." I should like to know what is meant by "compensatory adjustments." Does it mean that the farmers, the lumbermen, the miners and the fishermen of Canada are to be given the same treatment as the manufacturers of Canada? Does it mean that these
people are to be allowed their cost of production with a reasonable advance for selling costs and profit? What a hope that would be, Mr. Speaker! Of course we know it is absurd to imagine that such a thing would be done.
There is no use in endeavouring to spread a disease of this kind in the country. It is now a cancer on the body politic; it is time we put the X-ray on it. That is the reason I ask for this committee. It may take a major operation to correct the disease, but we are fast approaching the point where it will be a question of kill or cure.
Referring now to the fixing of the value for duty purposes in combination with antidumping legislation covering imports competing with goods made in Canada, in 1922 an amendment to the Customs Act was passed which gave the minister power to set values for duty purposes and thereby imposed the anti-dumping legislation in order to protect natural products of a class or kind grown or produced in Canada. The purpose of the legislation at that time was to protect growers of fruits and vegetables in this country from undue importations while the Canadian farmers' crops were moving to market. In 1930 this section was amended to cover any goods imported and sold or on consignment under such conditions as would prejudicially or injuriously affect the interest of producers or manufacturers, the minister being given the right to fix the values, and the values so fixed to be construed as the fair market value. Here was the final blow for the importer. He had to guess what the minister and his officials had in their minds and what they would do before he was able to import goods. This amendment was certainly designed and passed to hinder and restrict the flow of trade.
In 1934 the section was amended so that it would not affect empire goods. In 1936 it was again amended, this time to give an importer the opportunity to appeal to the tariff board against the value fixed, but the uncertainties regarding valuation still persist and constitute a decidedly limiting factor in respect to the importation of goods into Canada. By the provisions of this section the minister may fix the value for duty of any goods and his valuation shall be the fair market value. Under this section, in 1937 the minister was given authority to make regional tariffs on fruits and vegetables, and under this section also there was brought down an amendment which, as I read it, certainly amazes me. It is section 43a(l) of the Customs Act:
All values for duty heretofore fixed by or on a basis or by a method prescribed by the minister or the commissioner of customs-

The Customs Tariff

Mark those words.
-or the assistant commissioner of customs, acting or purporting to act pursuant to the provisions of section forty-seven A of the Customs Act, chapter forty-eight of the revised statutes of Canada, 1906, as enacted by section three of chapter eighteen of the statutes of 1922, or of section forty-three of the Customs Act, chapter forty-two of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, or of section forty-three-
And so on with different sections. In other words this was an admission to parliament that although parliament had delegated powers -the widest kinds of powers-to the national revenue department, when they were given those powers they did not stay within them, and the minister had to come to this house and have an amending section passed to sanction the actions of the officials of the department and clothe them with the authority of parliament. Under this section our one hundred dollars' worth of goods becomes whatever the minister, the commissioner of customs or the assistant commissioner of customs wishes to increase it to.
In conjunction with all these sections of the Customs Act there is section 6 of the Customs Tariff, which is the anti-dumping legislation. It first made its appearance in 1904. It was placed there for the purpose of protecting Canadian manufacturers against actual dumping based on the then Customs Act, which placed the value as the value for export in the country of origin. It could not at that time be placed against the free list but only against dutiable goods, and at that time, if any article carried a tariff or combination of tariffs which amounted to fifty per cent ad valorem, the dumping duty could not be applied at all. Besides, it was limited to fifteen per cent as an advance for duty purposes.
In 1907 this section was changed to apply to the free list as well as to the dutiable list. In 1930 a major revision of section 6 of the Customs Tariff took place, which altered the whole basis of tariff making in Canada. This section overrides the whole Customs Act and Customs Tariff in the addition of values and the application of the dumping duty. The increased valuation for duty purposes now becomes proof of dumping, and superduties are imposed. The imposition of an ad valorem tariff of fifty per cent, which previously had exempted the article, was thereby cancelled. The maximum advance for duty purposes of fifteen per cent became fifty per cent. If the invoice for goods to an importer were less than the fair market value of the same article when sold for home consumption in the country of origin, or less

than the fair market value as determined under sections 36 and 41, or less than the fair market value fixed under sections 37 or 43, a dumping duty was applied equal to the difference between the invoice price and the fair market value so fixed. In other words, the definition of dumping was altogether changed. Once the department said that the value should be higher, immediately and automatically the dumping duty came into play.
Now take our example, one hundred dollars' worth of goods. Parliament says the tariff rate shall be forty per cent. Value fixed, $200; duty at forty per cent, $80; dumping duty, fifty per cent of the increase, $50, a total of $130, or 130 per cent. Remember also that the import excise tax of three per cent goes on the whole amount of $230 and becomes seven per cent instead of three per cent, making it $137. Add that to the original value of $100 and you have $237 upon which the eight per cent sales tax is computed, instead of $140 as parliament intended it to be.
In 1936 this section was amended to determine what were made in Canada goods. It was established that thenceforth not less than ten per cent of Canadian consumption must be produced in Canada before goods could be classed as made in Canada goods. But, Mr. Speaker, we are still in this position, that one hundred per cent of the consumption of these goods manufactured in Canada must be charged higher prices because the duty must be raised and dumping duties applied in order to protect ten to fifteen per cent of the production which is made in Canada.
Under this protective tariff system we have a system of drawbacks on goods for reexport, and it has the effect of defeating the protection given to certain Canadian industries who produce goods needed by other Canadian manufacturers for their finished articles. The Canadian manufacturer wants protection only one way. He does not want to pay for it on anything he has to buy; he wants it to be paid only on what he has to sell. Therefore when certain goods are purchased by the manufacturer which go into the production of goods that are to be exported, instead of buying from the Canadian protected manufacturer he buys the goods from some other country and claims and receives a drawback thereon.
In addition, there are drawbacks on home consumption goods. You will find several pages of them at the back of the Customs Tariff. These are used in order that some manufacturer in Canada who is producing articles which are not protected, articles which

The Customs Tariff
are on the free list, may be able to import goods that are protected and use them in his own goods which are not protected; or it may be that there is a lower tariff on the finished article made in Canada, than there is on the partly finished article entering into its manufacture. Therefore the drawback is allowed in these cases.
But, Mr. Speaker, there is another use for the drawback: when the Minister of Finance lowers the protection on the finished article to the Canadian manufacturer, he can return to him a large part by giving him a drawback on imported goods that enter into the manufacture of home consumed goods. 'Under these circumstances under our protective system it is the greatest wheedler w'ho gets the drawback.
We should look into this matter also to determine whether all the drawbacks that are claimed and paid should be claimed and paid. I contend it is a pretty difficult thing to determine whether the conditions set before the department are really the true conditions, and what brings that to my mind is evidence that came out in regard to certain gentlemen engaged in the textile industry who came to this government and told them they were going to be swamped by the importation of certain goods, and it was found out later that no such condition obtained.
In conclusion, the purpose of my resolution is to prove to parliament and the country that parliament has delegated to departmental officials important taxing powers of parliament, and that this procedure is not in the best interests of the people of Canada.
I ask for a committee for the purpose of bringing before parliament practical men engaged in the importing business to show from their records and from their statements under oath whether or not this delegation of power has had a bad effect on the business life of the people of Canada; to what extent it has raised prices on home manufactured goods to the consumer, and to show that it has lowered the purchasing power of the consumer.
I say to the Minister of National Revenue that the Customs Act and the Customs Tariff have placed upon his shoulders a responsibility that should never have been placed upon the shoulders of any man in Canada. Parliament, through these acts, sir, has directed him to see that the interests of certain Canadian producers or manufacturers shall not be prejudicially or injuriously affected by the importation of goods. There is not one word of direction in those acts in regard to the interests of the great consuming public.
These directions defeat the aims of democracy, they take away majority rights and substitute therefor privileges for a small minority. They take from one section of Canada and give to another. They are the negation of freedom; they are the negation of liberalism; they are the means of regimentation of the people; they are the cause of a lower standard of living throughout Canada. They are the main cause of unemployment in the great basic industries of this country. They are unduly restricting and unduly complicating the import and, thereby, the export trade upon which the large percentage of our people live. They maintain prices of imported goods and eliminate healthy competition from abroad, which creates an artificial price level in Canada. They hinder, delay and discourage the flow of imported goods. They cause ill-will toward Canada in the countries where we hope to sell large quantities of our farm products and the products of our mines, forests and fisheries.
These acts are older than some of the infant industries which they are framed to protect ad infinitum.
It is time, Mr. Speaker, that this parliament looked into these matters. It is time we closely considered revamping these acts and making them conform with conditions and needs of the year 1938. Let parliament take back the powers that have been delegated to departmental officials.
As a member of parliament I protest against this way of carrying on the country's business, and I ask parliament to consider this resolution in the best interests of the people of Canada.

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext:
In rising to second this resolution, Mr. Speaker, I am sure it is entirely needless for me to say that there is no intention on my part- and I know there was none in the minds of those who framed and put the resolution on the order paper-to reflect in any way on the minister (Mr. Ilsley) or his officials, or on their integrity, their intelligence and sense of fair play. Particularly would that not be the case in reference to a minister who during the past few years has made for himself a record which probably has not been excelled by any other minister of the crown administering the customs department since confederation. Every member of this house knows something at least of the burdens that have been cast upon his shoulders, which, as the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) has said, should never have been placed on the shoulders of any one man in Canada.
The Cm toms Tariff

So far as the officers of the department are concerned, I have less acquaintance with them, but I am just as well satisfied that they are doing everything to the best of their ability to carry out the system under which they are working.
The department that we are asked to investigate is something like Topsy in Uncle Tom's Cabin. It never was made; it just "growed." And the hide-holes and all the rest of it grew up along with it as a result of conditions about which it is needless to speak at the moment.
My opinion with regard to matters of this kind is that it should not require a special motion or resolution of the House of Commons to ensure investigation of departments from time to time. I believe that every department should be subject to investigation by the House of Commons at regular intervals in order to familiarize members with the conduct of business in the various branches of government, to familiarize the heads of departments with the intent of parliament and to familiarize the country with both. It would also enable us to get the reaction of the country to the conduct of affairs if such investigations were carried out openly by members of parliament. I submit that it should be done, and I believe that the time is coming when it will be done.
When the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) was Minister of Agriculture he did everything he could in this house, everything that lay within his power, to bring about a thorough investigation by the House of Commons of his own department, from year to year. I remember sitting where I am now and listening to the minister, as he then was, putting through his estimates. Opposition members would call "Carried" and [ remember the then minister saying, "No, t is not carried, and it is not going to be carried until more is told of the work of this department, because this is the only occasion on which that work can be made known to the country."
I suggest that there is no reflection on any department of government in the request for an investigation from time to time for the purpose of familiarizing members of the House of Commons with the detailed operations of that department. In the past twelve years, that is to say, since I first entered this house, and in the intervening years during my absence, I have not known ten per cent of the members of the house, including myself *-and I have a fair acquaintance among the members-who were familiar with the detailed workings of the department which we are discussing at the moment. I remarked this

to one of my colleagues this morning and he said that I would be safe in cutting the percentage down to five or even less. This is an extremely important department. I do not believe there is another one that touches the people more closely or one with which they are more concerned, except, possibly, the Department of Justice. Some people may think it strange that I should rate these two departments as I do, but in my opinion the Department of Justice is, if anything, the most important of all the departments inasmuch as it so closely affects the life and liberty of the subject. I repeat, the collecting of revenues, and the opportunity to assist or to hinder industry as the case may be, make this an extremely important department.
I will not discuss the question of revenues at the moment, but if I have time later on I will touch upon it. I find, however, that there is considerable bewilderment in the country on the part of some would-be importers with regard to what they have to pay for certain goods, the classification of those goods, and charges and so on. I submit that it is time that the state of uncertainty in this connection was removed. Some years ago I had an inquiry from a would-be importer who wanted to bring in a certain article from the United States to Vancouver. I took the matter up with the department and could not possibly get a rate that would be satisfactorily definite to this man. This was many years ago but I am satisfied that the same condition has prevailed more or less in the years in between. This fact is a source of trouble to a great many people, particularly those in the primary industries. By primary industries I do not mean the farmers of any particular type but all the primary industries, because they are all affected by the customs tariff in the conduct of their business. Of course, this department touches every individual in his purchase of goods.
I am told sometimes that it is better to hide taxes, to cover them up so that the people will not be conscious of what they are paying; but in the process they grow immensely, just as some plants do when you cover them up. If you cover certain plants with the proper material and leave them under proper conditions as to temperature, air and humidity they grow very fast. These charges in connection with the tariff grow apace pretty much in the same way, and for that reason the Chancellor of the Exchequer in Great Britain was right when he said, " I could tax the shirts off the backs of the people of these islands and they would never know what was happening to them if I were allowed to do it by indirect means."

The Customs Tariff
As regards added charges such as I have mentioned, I will not go into any details but I have here a page from one of the oldest newspapers in Canada, the Montreal Daily Herald, of Thursday, November 18, 1937. I find quotations on various cars blazoned all over the page. I will quote a few to show what the tariff does to the people and how important are the operations of the Department of National Revenue. What I am about to quote will convince the house, I believe, of the importance of knowing the workings of the department. There should be no room for suspicion in the mind of anyone that any charge is being made in that department except such as is sanctioned by the parliament of Canada.
I will take one or two motor cars, not manufactured in Canada, at any rate so far as I know. For the Cadillac V-8, 60 type, touring sedan, the price quoted at the New York motor show held not long ago was $2,085, while in Canada the Montreal price was $2,450, according to this reputable newspaper. For the LaSalle V-8 coupe, two passenger, the price in New York was $1,300, and in Montreal $1,890. I do not believe that that car is made in Canada. I am taking the prices at random. Take the Hudson Six types. For the coupe, three passenger, the New York price was $909, and the Montreal price $1,255. For the custom eight touring brougham, capacity six, the New York price was $1,155, and the Montreal price $1,565. The Chrysler, a favourite Canadian make, is quoted at the New York show at $918, while the Montreal price was $1,230. These prices are for the business coupe. The coupe is $963 in New York, and $1,301 in Montreal.

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext:
If the $1,301 is for a used car it is still worse. The car will give good service, there is no dispute about quality with respect to these cars, the question is one of price. Take the Chrysler Imperial Eight types. The business coupe, capacity two, was $1,123 in New York, and $1,559 in Montreal.
It might be fair to touch on some of the more commonly sold cars, because, after all, these prices affect a good many people. Let us take the Chevrolet. The Master town sedan was quoted at Plattsburg, New York, at $732, and the Montreal price is $1,040. The coupe de luxe at Plattsburg is $775, and in Montreal $955. I find here a car described as the universal car, a new Ford. The price in Plattsburg of the standard coupe, 85 horsepower, is $688, and in Montreal, $867. The
4-door sedan de luxe, 85 horsepower, five passenger, is $836 in Plattsburg and $1,052 in Canada.
There are many others I could quote; the difference in price is pretty much the same. I will not take up time reading more prices, however. I will simply observe that the people have to face these vast differences, while in many instances the goods they import are of a kind not made in this countiy. We must all realize, I am sure, how important it is to this house to know the workings of a department of this kind; they should be thoroughly understood, both inside and out. Such a department should live in a glass house open to the public, so that the people might become familiar with its operations. There would then be no room for suspicion, and no one would fear that conditions not sanctioned by parliament existed.
There is another consideration. It is important for Canada that the maximum amount of revenue be collected by the department. Someone might tell me that the argument that the department should collect as much as possible is a strange one for me to use. I say it is important that the maximum revenue be collected. I know of only one way to bring that about, that is to allow the business to increase to its natural maximum, not to put any difficulties in the way. Everyone knows there is a maximum point, which is reached when conditions are mutually satisfactory. A lowering of price may bring more profit, but prices may be lowered too much and so a loss entailed. But there is always a point where price and cost and bulk of sales coincide to ensure the highest profit or the highest revenue. For that reason I believe this matter should be checked up very closely.
I have in my hand an official document, the report of the proceedings of a committee of the house, from which I should like to read three paragraphs. It is the report of the special committee on farm implement prices which sat last year. At page 1295 it says:
20.	That regulations of the Department of National Revenue, under the above provisions, have resulted in the inequality of treatment of importers of a like class and that the whole matter should be the subject of survey by the minister of that department.
21.	That these regulations have resulted directly and indirectly in the retention in the United States of profits arising out of the operations in Canada of certain United States companies and that these profits have been subjected to income tax in the United States instead of in Canada.
The Customs Tariff

22.	Tliat indirectly this retention of profits in the United States affected the price level of farm implements in Canada as the true profits arising out of their Canadian operations were not properly appreciated by the United States companies.
Two things have happened; prices of farm implements have been held at a higher level than they might otherwise have been, and revenue that should have been collected in Canada was collected in another country, a very undesirable condition of affairs.
I believe that a very interesting statement which I read the other day is true. It is found in a book by Albert Edward Wiggam entitled Marks of an Educated Man. The writer says:
The highest possible philanthropy and program of social welfare and moral uplift is the scientific organization of business. I think it is. We are in a business world, and when that business is badly organized everyone suffers. When business is efficiently organized everybody benefits.
I have not said that the business of this department is badly organized; but in view of what has taken place, I say it should be investigated by the house. The other day when the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) was advocating in the house a regional tariff under the Department of National Revenue there was a good deal of opposition expressed in a nice way to that proposal. But we have had now for some years a regional tariff or a system of regional tariffs in Canada. I think it is the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) we have to thank for that; I believe it was during his administration that regional tariffs were first adopted. Whether that is so or not, the principle has been adopted that not all tariffs are suited to conditions everywhere in this country. It is true that at the present time the regional tariff is confined largely to natural products; but there is no reason why, once the principle is conceded, it could not be extended along other lines.
Let me refer for a moment to other difficulties, other anomalies in the administration of the tariff. At page 948 of the proceedings of the committee on farm implement prices the witness, an official of the department, who was trying his best to give that committee a picture of things as they are, was asked:
Q. There has been no change since that time?
A. No.
Q. For Massey-Harris, that constitutes the position to date?	_
A. To date, the present ruling on which Massey-Harris are '-iporting.
[Mr. M. McLean. 1
Q. As compared with International Harvester Company-International Harvester Company get a twenty-five per cent discount on implements ?
A. Right.
Q. On tractors International Harvester Company get what?
A. Twenty per cent on all tractors except model WD40 on which the discount is twenty-five per cent.
Q. And on repairs International Harvester Company get what?
A. Repairs to above machines, consumers' list price less discount of thirty-five and twenty-five.
Q. What would that net? Will you figure that out, please ?
A. Fifty-one and one-quarter per cent.
Q. As compared with the net which you gave us of 42-62?
Mr. Macdonald: What you are talking about there, about the reduced price, the discount is 49-75.
That is said by one member of the committee. Another member said, "No." The witness answered, "fifty-one and one-quarter." Counsel for the committee said, "The discount is fifty-one and one-quarter."
Q. That is International Harvester Company? A. Yes.
Q. And the Massey-Harris figure, net, you gave a few minutes ago was what?
And the answer was, "42-62," as against 51| in the case of the other company. I shall read a paragraph or two more in order to indicate how that difficulty came about. Counsel for the committee asked:
Q. I must confess, Mr. Hooper, I do not follow you. If you take Massey-Harris Company in Canada, they allow their dealers a less commission than the International Harvester Company for the reason that the Massey-Harris absorb some of the local freight from the dealer to his customer. The International Harvester Company do not. They expect the dealer to take care of that unless he can pass it on to the farmer. So that their discount allowed by a company, but which is less than another company, is usually compensated by some other feature of the contract. _ Why would the department make a distinction between Massey-Harris and the International Harvester Company on a tractor or an implement or a part of either of equal quality value? Why should there be any difference at the port of entry when the Massey-Harris present, let us say for the purpose of argument, to bring it out clearly, a binder of equal quality value? Why should there be any difference in the basis on which that binder enters Canada in the percentage of fair market value of that binder in the United States?
A. The answer to that is, I think, that in 1935 the International Harvester Company became aware that that portion of the law requiring the value for duty purposes to be no less than the wholesale price had been repealed, and they requested the department to study their situation and consider whether a greater discount could not be given than the one under

The Customs Tariff
*which they were operating. That study was made, and the discount was established at twenty per cent off dealers' price and subsequently to twenty-five per cent. The Massey-Harris Company did not request any lower value for duty purposes than they had been operating on since 1917 and did not ask for any better discount than they allowed in their own sales in the United States, and we have accepted the price at which they sell to others in the United States as establishing the value for duty purposes.
Q. With the result that the department, while it changed its policy, or the basis on which it applied the existing law to the International Harvester, did not think it was their duty to pass that on to other members of the industry as a general ruling rather than a specific ruling applying to only one company?
A. No, we did not; and only now the department has lately under consideration a system whereby we would give one ruling to the entire industry. That has been the policy which has been advocated in the department, but it has not- yet been approved. It would be a departure from the procedure of years.
Q. You see what a very great weapon is placed in the hands of the administrative department of the government?
A. Oh, yes.
Q. You can see that?
A. I quite see that.
That bears out what I said, that it would be a departure from the procedure of years, that this was not framed specifically to do things it was meant to do, but, like Topsy, it " just growed."
I should like to continue with many more extracts of the same nature to prove to the hilt the contention we are making, that it is time to bring about a change in matters of this kind. I shall read just a few lines more from the proceedings before the same committee sitting the next day to that fiom which I have quoted. A request for information by correspondence was put in, and I want to say that the officials of the department had, probably rightly, refused to bring it in, but the minister saw that whatever was requested by the committee was promptly placed before it. I want to thank him now as I did then for his cooperation with the committee at every stage of the inquiry that we were conducting. But a matter of rubber tires for tractors came up, and the witness did not have the correspondence with him on the night in question. So on March 30, as reported at page 995, an explanation was given as to changes affecting rubber tires. The following letter was addressed to the chairman of the committee:
In respect to rubber tires for use on internal combustion traction engines, concerning which I gave evidence before the committee on Wednesday the 24th instant, I may state that these articles were first ruled as admissible as complete parts of the tractors on the 28th March,
1933.	A copy of this ruling is attached. This carried on until June 1936, when the ruling was changed classifying such rubber tires under tariff item 618b.
The oommittee has asked what brought about the change in the ruling. In this connection, after going over the files, and discussing the matter with the commissioner of customs and the dominion customs appraiser, I find that in the latter part of May or early in June, 1936, the commissioner of customs was interviewed with respect to this ruling by Mr. Berkenshaw, sales manager of the Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company Limited, and Mr. A. R. Caldwell, customs manager of that company. I believe the commissioner was also interviewed subsequently by either one or both of these gentlemen. The commissioner was unaware of the existing ruling and after examining the tariff files containing the ruling was of the opinion that the ruling was not correct, that the articles were more definitely covered by the provision in tariff item 618b for rubber tires, and changed the ruling in a letter to the Firestone Tire & Rubber Company of Canada Limited, dated the 10th June, 1936, file No. 181155. I am herewith submitting copies of representative departmental letters on this matter, including the letter to Firestone Tire & Rubber Company of Canada Limited and previous letters on the subject. There are, of course, other letters but they are all of a similar nature.
I want to point out that the date on which that change was made is significant. Apparently the minister was not aware of it; there is nothing said about that, though naturally he will feel obliged to take responsibility for it. Later on, in answer to questions by myself, this is the evidence that was given:
Q. I am referring now solely to farm tractors, free of duty, coming in with iron tires. Now, later on the manufacturers put on rubber tires?
A. Yes.
Q. Was there any difference made at any time at the beginning with regard to the importation of rubber tired tractors?
A. No. From the first time the question arose the department ruled that the big low-pressure tires that were adapted only for use on tractors were a complete part of the tractor.
Q. That was always free?
A. On the ones under $1,400.
Q. Yes, of course. Then, later on when they began importing tires for repair purposes, for replacement purposes, were they free at any time?
A. The same situation followed through.
Q. What made the change that caused the appeal to be made to the Tariff Board?
A. Well, the department in its wisdom decided it might not be right and they changed.
Q. First, they decided they were free?
A. Yes.
Q. And then they decided they were dutiable, and then an appeal was made to the tariff board, and the result of that appeal was respected and they were brought in free?
A. Yes.
Q. When would you say that the change was made from free to dutiable?
A. I think it was in June, 1936.
The Customs Tariff

Q. June, 1936, that they were made dutiable?
A. Yes.
Q. Will you tell me how the department made up its mind or came to that conclusion?
A. Well, the tire item is not what we call an n.o.p. item. That is items which are general items and which are not all inclusive. The abbreviation "n.o.p." means "not otherwise provided for." We have an item 618-B which reads, "tires for vehicles of all kinds" without that abbreviation "n.o.p." And after we reviewed the case we decided that maybe we were not right; that it was a specific item and that the tires were actually specifically provided for there and we accordingly changed our ruling.
Q. Would you mind answering me two questions in that respect? I should like to know who made the first ruling and who appealed against that ruling, how the appeal came to be made that led to the reconsideration of the item, and then who made the item dutiable without apparently getting a legal interpretation, or if you did get a legal interpretation from the justice department, I should like to know the history?
A. We did not get a legal interpretation.
So a ruling that had held for some years was thrown into the discard apparently because a representative of a tire and rubber company came along and convinced the department that that should be done. A little later in the same day the question as to how this came about was still being gone into. The witness was not quite sure; but a former minister of trade and commerce, the present hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) was a member of the committee, and he said:
I think we can get at it, a blind man almost could get at it; one of the tire companies applied for it. I don't suppose there is any doubt about it. Bring the record and let us see it. I think Mr. McLean has put his finger on a very important thing. What right has the dominion appraiser or anybody else got to change an existing practice established under a law made by parliament?
The greatest significance there lies in the fact that at the time, in June, 1936, when that change was made by the commissioner and the customs appraiser, at the request of an official of a tire and rubber company, this house was sitting. Hon. gentlemen were here, and they had authority to deal with the matter, if it was considered necessary that that should be done. The result of changes of this kind means that a bureaucracy is growing up in our country. Our people do not trust bureaucracies. They have the wisdom of centuries behind them in refusing to do so, because under bureaucracies changes can be made otherwise than in the full light of day. This is bad for the country and bad for the morale of the officials. I am satisfied that it is bad for administration and, as the

hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) said, it puts an intolerable load on any minister of the day.
I hold in my hand a few thoughts along that line written by one of the most prominent men of Great Britain which, however, I am not going to read at length. Lord Hewart of Bury is the author of a book entitled The New Despotism, and hon. members would find their time well spent if they looked over some of the arguments contained therein. Lord Hewart deals with an act of parliament that was passed in 1925, which gave to the minister in charge of municipal affairs-that is not his correct title, of course-power to remove, by order, any difficulty which might arise in the application of the act, together with other powers. Lord Hewart points out that the case would have to be serious before any minister would actually undertake to use such powers; nevertheless those powers were given to a minister. The learned writer of the book thought it quite extraordinary that parliament should confer that power on any minister for a period of four years. As the hon. member for Moose Jaw has shown, this power has been growing in Canada since confederation, and is not limited to any particular period. The court in Britain before which an action arising under the act was heard, made this reference in its unanimous judgment:
This I think, though I say it with some hesitation, may be regarded as indicating the high water mark of legislative provisions of this character. It is obvious that if this court had taken another view of the case presented to us to-day and had decided to quash this order as having been made ultra vires, the minister might to-morrow, under the provisions of section 67, have arrived at the same end by making an order and removing the difficulty.
Then Lord Hewart went on:
Now it will probably be admitted that matters must have gone rather far before a minister thought fit to propose, and parliament, either deliberately or by inadvertence, consented to approve a scheme that empowered a government department, on grounds of expediency, to make departmental orders modifying the provisions of the statute which conferred the power. A little inquiry will serve to show that there is now, and for some years past has been, a persistent influence at work which, whatever the motives or the intentions that support it may be thought to be, undoubtedly has the effect of placing a large and increasing field of departmental authority and activity beyond the reach of the ordinary law. Whether this influence ought to be encouraged, or whether it ought rather to be checked and limited, are questions into which, for the moment, it is not necessary to enter. But it does at least seem desirable that the influence itself should be clearly discerned, that its essential nature and tendency should be quite

The Customs Tariff
plainly exhibited, and that its various methods and manifestations should not be allowed to continue and multiply under a cloak of obscurity.
And mark this, Mr. Speaker:
The citizens of a state may indeed believe or boast that, at a given moment, they enjoy, or at any rate possess, a system of representative institutions, and that the ordinary law of the land, interpreted and administered by the regular courts, is comprehensive enough and strong enough for all its proper purposes. But their belief will stand in need of revision if, in truth and in fact, an organized and diligent minority, equipped with convenient drafts, and employing after a fashion part of the machinery of representative institutions, is steadily increasing the range and the power of departmental authority and withdrawing its operations more and more from the jurisdiction of the courts.
Later on, dealing with very much the same thing, he adds:
But other considerations apply if a mass of evidence establishes the fact that there is in existence a persistent and well contrived system, intended to produce, and in practice producing. a despotic power which at one and the same time places government departments above the sovereignty of parliament and beyond the jurisdiction of the courts. If it appears that this system springs from and depends upon a deep seated official conviction, which in turn it nourishes and strengthens by each successive manifestation of its vigour, and this, when all is said and done, is the best and most scientific way of ruling the country, the consequences, unless they are checked, must be in the highest degree formidable.
That there is in existence, and in certain quarters in the ascendant, a genuine belief that parliamentary institutions and the rule of law have been tried and found wanting, and that the time has come for the departmental despot, who shall be at once scientific and benevolent, but above all a law to himself, needs no demonstration. There is an agreeable story, not too old, of a distinguished Anglo-Indian civilian, who, returning home on leave after a prolonged absence, passed the houses of parliament on his way from Victoria to Charing Cross. "What place is that?" he asked. "That, sir," was the answer, "is parliament-the houses of parliament." "Really," he exclaimed, though his exclamation was in fact slightly different, "does that rubbish still go on?" Everybody knows the frame of mind, and everybody has met some of the teachers in that school.
But another aspect of the matter is illustrated by a well known conversation which took place, not so many years ago, between a distinguished treasury official, if the epithet is not tautologous, and the Chancellor of the Exchequer. It happened that matters had not gone quite smoothly in the House of Commons that evening. The departmental specialist was not, for once, able to say to his chief, after the rising of the house, with that air which as nearly approaches a tone of triumph as official decorum permits, "well, sir, we have got our clauses." What he did say was that he wondered whether all this palaver was really
necessary. After all, what was the good of the House of Commons? And how perfectly useless was the House of Lords! Why should the work of the expert be always at the merey of the ignorant amateur? Why should people be allowed to try to govern themselves when it was manifestly so much better for them to be governed by those who knew how to govern? "Seriously," he asked, "could not this country be governed by the civil service?" "Undoubtedly it could," replied the Chancellor of the Exchequer, "undoubtedly it could. And I am quite sure that you and your colleagues would govern the country remarkably well. But let me tell you this, my young friend: at the end of six months of it. there would not be enough lamp posts in Whitehall to go round."
I know that officials of the Canadian civil service do not look on the public business of Canada in that way, nor do they take that attitude towards the House of Commons, but there is always a possibility of bureaucratic methods developing when there is more or less of a mystery about rulings made by departments. With the multitude of rules and changes and classifications in the work of this department, it is possible that that is what might happen. It is all important for this country, from the standpoint of trade and industry and revenue, that there should be no suspicion of that kind. It is too important that the people of this country should retain their faith in democratic government wherein all the people are represented and wherein all the members of parliament take part in making the laws. For this and other reasons, I second the motion which has been proposed.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the
tone of the two speeches that have just been made in support of this resolution. On reading the resolution some time ago I thought that possibly an attack upon the administration of the department was to be made, but hon. members who have addressed the house have made it abundantly clear that they have in mind defects in the system rather than the administration of the system by the department. I am pleased that that is the case because, having had two years' experience as the head of the Department of National Revenue, and having worked with the senior and other officials of the departs ment, I have no hesitation in paying them a sincere tribute for their efficiency, for their honesty and for their integrity and bona fides. I have come in contact with many hon. members of the house in connection with departmental matters and also with many members of the business public of Canada and I think it is safe to say that the Department of National Revenue now commands and has
The Customs Tariff

commanded for years the respect of the business and industrial communities of Canada.
I should like to make a few observations with regard to the criticisms of the system that have been made by the mover of the resolution. I believe the house realizes that this is an intricate and difficult subject with which to deal. I am afraid it is also a dry subject and that being the case I do not intend to read any of the sections of the act or any of the regulations passed under the provisions of the act. I want to express in the simplest possible language-language that will be understood by laymen generally-the principles that underlie the Customs Act.
The officials and the minister of the Department of National Revenue have to do with two difficult classes of problems, that is, with valuations and classifications. The mover of the resolution referred mainly to valuations, while the seconder had something to say about classifications. Needless to say investigations must be made and decisions rendered from time to time by the senior officials and the minister in classifying goods under one or another of the items of the customs tariff and in valuing goods for duty purposes. I do not know of any system of customs administration that would get rid of the necessity of these departmental decisions.
For instance, take one matter referred to this afternoon by the seconder of the resolution. He referred to the classification of rubber tires for tractors. In this connection representations had been made to the department, and the senior officials, in the course of their respective duties, were convinced that a mistake had been made. They altered the classification, just as has been done from time to time in connection with other items. Otherwise it would be impossible for the business of the department to go on. An appeal was taken from this decision to the tariff board and the tariff board supported the decision in part and reversed it in part, and the matter was settled. The case was a fairly normal one, and I do not know of any system of customs administration in the world which would do away with the necessity of decisions of this kind being made by departmental officials.
I want to refer now to valuations. The basis of our system of valuations is a rule which has been established in this country since at least 1883, that the value for duty purposes shall be the fair market value of the goods, when sold for home consumption, in the market whence they were imported. I know that many Canadian people believe that

the ad valorem rate is reckoned upon the cost of the goods imported. They think that if goods can be bought for one dollar in another country and the rate of duty is twenty per cent, the duty will be twenty cents. That is an inaccurate way of stating the case. The basis of our valuation for duty purposes is not the invoice price, not the cost; it is the home market value. As I say, this has been the case for the last fifty-five years, and I believe the same rule applies in other countries. If this is to be continued as the basis of our customs valuations, it then follows that investigations must take place and decisions be arrived at as to what is the home market value.

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext: What does the minister mean by "home"?

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext: I mean the value in the country of origin, the country whence the goods were shipped at the time they were shipped to Canada. This is defined very precisely in section 35 of the act.

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext: Is that the selling price at home?

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext: It is the fair home market value.

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext: Would that be the selling price?

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext: It is not necessarily the selling price, as I shall explain in a minute. In perhaps ninety-five per cent of the cases the home market value would be the invoice price, but there are some cases in which the two prices would not correspond. There are of course levels of prices in the home market, but that opens up another question into which I did not think it would be necessary to go this afternoon.

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext: Does that also apply to valuations made on used cars coming into Canada?

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext: Used cars are prohibited.

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext: When they do come in.

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext:
With the hon. gentleman's permission, I will ask the house to keep in mind section 35, which contains the rule to which I refer and which is the basic, fundamental rule of customs administration. There are two or three other sections, 36 and 41 and 43, which the house might also bear in mind. Sections 36 and 41 are subsidiary to section 35 and really are designed to carry out the purposes of section 35. Section 36 provides that the value for duty shall not be less than the cost of production in the country of

The Customs Tariff
origin, plus a reasonable advance for selling cost or profit. That section is based upon the theory that the selling in the home market at less than cost of production plus reasonable advance is a temporary selling, a distress affair, a practice which if continued will put those selling the goods into bankruptcy and should not be accepted by this country as the fair home market value. That is the purpose of section 36. In the administration of that section, if the department receives a complaint that goods imported into this country are being purchased at less than the cost of production plus a reasonable advance, it is necessary for the department to make investigation as to the cost of production in the country of origin, prepare a report and then, possibly, make a ruling. So there again is the necessity of departmental or ministerial investigation and decision.

speechtext: Who determines the cost of production in the home market?

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext: The departmental officials. The application of it is very limited. Investigation is made upon complaint, and it is a very minor, subsidiary section.
