Ordinarily the complaint
would come from Canadian competitors of the foreign suppliers.

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext: I thought so.

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext: Why would it not?

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext: I do not understand why they should not complain if they want to.

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext:
The question I raised is due to this. Suppose a manufacturer is bringing in raw material for his own use, and a competitor complains; where does he get his information? How does he get the information about the importation of which he complains?	From the departmental
officials?

subtopic: MOTION FOR COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE APPLICATION AND COLLECTION OF DUTIES AND PRACTICE RESPECTING DRAWBACKS
speechtext:
There are various ways in which he might realize that importations were taking place at a low price. He would know the price at which they were being resold in Canada. There are complaints, anyway.
So much for section 36. The third section I referred to was section 41. That section applies to cases where there is no established home market value, and to certain other peculiar cases, and under the circumstances outlined in the section the minister is authorized to fix a fair value. The principles upon which values are fixed have been worked out with great care by the department over
a period of years and so far as I know there is no secret as to what those principles are. As I have said, section 41 is not very important, but it is necessary because, if there is no home market value, if there is no consumption in the home market, or if goods are not sold in the home market under conditions similar to those which govern their importation into this country, somebody has to fix what is the fair value for importation.
Another section of the act, namely section 43, is based upon entirely different principles; it permits the Minister of National Revenue, under the authorization of the governor in council, to make arbitrary valuations. It is at variance with the principle underlying the Customs Act. This section was inserted a few years ago. The history of it was given this afternoon by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross). During the last two years it has fallen almost into disuse except in respect of fruits and vegetables, but it is applied to those articles and is the only system that we have been able to work out to control their importation, if it is desirable to control it. I do not know of any better system. At any rate that is the main function of section 43.
When this government assumed office there were between twenty-five and thirty-five valuations of manufactured goods under section 43. With the exception of three, these have all been cancelled in so far as importations from countries entitled to the benefits of the most favoured nation and intermediate tariffs are concerned. So the main use of the section is, as I have said, in its application to fruits and vegetables. Although this is a matter of policy, with which I as an administrator am not primarily concerned, I believe that the justification of this section for application to other than fruits and vegetables is as an emergency instrument. Indeed I applied it once for a short period as an emergency section, in regard to the importation of coronation souvenirs, and there was practically no complaint from the people of Canada. That was, I thought, a legitimate application of section 43, a section which is at variance, as I have said, with the principle of section 35.
In a reform of the Customs Act such as the mover of this resolution possibly has in mind, the first question that must be answered is this: Shall we retain or shall we abandon home market value as the basis of our customs valuation? Once that principle is decided everything else can follow along naturally. Some countries apply a different principle. Great Britain has as its basis cost plus insurance plus freight, and that system has some
The Customs Tariff

advantages. There is one disadvantage, in a country situated as Canada is, in this cost basis. A home market basis is very much harder to evade than a cost basis. A cost basis on customs valuation makes rebates as between purchaser and seller very much easier, and our geographical position is such that it would be, I feel sure, a very serious problem for Canada if Canada were to abandon the home market basis and adopt the cost basis.
In the administration of the Customs Act the government and the minister should keep in mind certain broad principles. The gentlemen who have spoken are quite right in saying that the act should not be administered, the tariff should not be applied, by the department primarily as an industry protecting device. The protective feature is of course present in our tariff, but the department is the Department of National Revenue, and our primary concern is to apply the tariff that we have to apply, to administer it strictly, regardless of the effects of its application on industry in the country or outside. It is very difficult to get people to appreciate or understand that point of view. We are continually being besought to place goods in a low classification because it would help the importer, or in a high because it would help the manufacturer; or we are asked to make a low valuation to help the importer or a high valuation to help the manufacturer. But these are not the considerations which should govern the department. These are matters which should be defined in the act, and then the act Should be strictly administered, because any other administration would be an unfair one.
I have laid down in two or three speeches that I have made on the subject of the department in the last two or three years the principles which I have tried to follow and have the officers of the department follow.
The first principle is that the department should be regarded primarily as a revenuecollecting agency, rather than as an industry-protecting agency. Protection of industry will follow collaterally, of course, because that is the design of a protective tariff; but our concern is to collect the revenue which the law says we shall collect, in accordance with the tariff.
The second principle is that no unnecessary administrative barrier shall be placed by the department in the way of imports. I am free to admit that the tariff can be administered in a way that will make importation difficult, and there have been times when this has been done. Your regulations may be so strict that certain commodities cannot be imported, and

delays in appraisals and various devices might be resorted to, if we wanted to do so, which would be technically within the law but would make importations difficult. That could be done under any system. Parliament cannot help it. It has to be left to the good sense and principles of the government of the day. But I do not think it is sound administration to erect unnecessary administrative barriers in the way of imports. In other words, we should not be astute to devise regulations within the law for keeping imports out, nor should we manipulate the law or regulations to do so. That principle has been laid down and is being followed by the department at the present time.
The third principle is that importers should be able to ascertain in advance, with as much certainty as possible, what they will be obliged to pay in the way of duties upon any importation. It is not possible to do that completely at times because they must be prepared to declare, and if necessary to show, that they are importing at the fair home market value. This may seem difficult to hon. members, but it is not so in practice. Usually importers will know pretty well the prevailing price in the country of origin, and if they import at that price they are safe; there is no question of what they have to pay. The instances given by the mover of the resolution, in which he got a forty per cent tariff up to a 150 per cent tariff, are supposititious cases; they are not actual cases, and I do not think they would happen in actual practice. If by $100 worth of goods he meant goods worth $100 in the home market, a forty per cent duty would mean that an importer would pay $40 not $100, $120 or $150. So I think the difficulties of administration in that respect were unduly stressed.

Rubber footwear is one of the three articles which are still subject to valuation under section 43. The value was lowered under the recent ruling because it was considered by the department that it was unduly high. That is substantially what was done in regard to rubber footwear.
Just one other matter. The impression was given, I fear, this afternoon, that the discretion of the officers of the department and of the minister is unchecked, unregulated, uncontrolled. Lord Hewart's book, The New Despotism, was cited, and the house was given to understand that we are a law unto ourselves. That statement should be qualified

The Customs Tariff
because, at every point where it has been possible to do so an appeal to a judicial tribunal has been provided. The old tribunal that heard the appeals was the board of customs, but since 1932 the tribunal which hears the appeals is the tariff board. The tariff board has a degree of permanency and a judicial cast which does not apply to the officers of the Department of National Revenue, who are crown officials collecting revenue for the crown; but the department's valuations, their made-in-Canada rulings, their classifications, their everything, in fact, except rulings under section 41, are all subject to appeal to the tariff board, and that has been provided by changes in the law or by order in council since the present government took office. So it is not correct to say that our discretion is uncontrolled or unregulated. Other countries have the same system.
As to the instances given to-day, it is only fair to say that we did not change the duty paid on rubber tires except in so far as we were right in doing so, because, as I say, an appeal has been provided to the tariff board.
Reference has been made to the home consumption drawback system. I do not know whether it is incumbent upon me to enter into a defence of that system; in fact, I do not know whether I believe in it or not myself. Under our tariff a great many articles are dutiable or not according to the use to which they are put after they are imported. The officials of the department do not like these items, and I do not like them, because they make it necessary for the department to police importers. When an importer says he is going to use a certain yarn for the manufacture of silk, and thereby gets it in free, it is necessary for the department to make a check on him to see that he uses it for that purpose and that he does not resell it. These are not regarded as desirable items from an administration standpoint. But I do not think it makes very much difference if you have items like that, once you admit the principle involved, because whether you do it by items in the customs tariff or by a system of domestic drawbacks the result is the same. As a matter of fact, the system of domestic drawbacks is safer for the crown because the crown collects the money in the first instance, and the importer is then obliged to show that he put the goods to the use which qualifies them for drawback of part of the duty before he can get that duty returned. I am sure, however, that the government will be prepared very seriously to consider a change, and perhaps a repeal, of the schedule
relating to domestic drawbacks. It might, however, entail the addition of a corresponding number of items in the customs tariff to effect the same end.
The mover of the resolution made some reference to the administration of drawbacks, and intimated that perhaps the greatest wheedlers got the most in drawbacks. I want to assure the house that the amount that an applicant for drawback gets does not in any sense depend upon his wheedling ability. The payment of drawbacks is much more severely and strictly regulated than that. Drawbacks are paid when proof is placed in the hands of the department that the goods qualify for drawback, and a large number of auditors check up on the facts that are presented to the department. After that the auditor general has access to our drawback records, and at times has questioned the payment of drawbacks by the department, whereupon the matter has been gone into anew to see that we were keeping strictly within the law. I do not believe that there is any looseness in the payment of drawbacks. The payment has to pass the treasury board and the auditor general, if he requests it, and council. It is regarded as an important matter to be paying these sums, and they are paid out in as strict a way as they would be paid out by any business institution in the country.
I come now to the specific proposal of the mover of the resolution, that is that the operations of the customs division be subject to review by a parliamentary committee. Personally I regard it as an unusual request, for this reason. Ordinarily, unless there is some charge of wrong-doing on the part of the officials of a certain department, one does not ask for a parliamentary committee to investigate that department. The hon. gentlemen who have spoken to-day have made it clear that they do not intimate or charge that anything of the sort has been done; they simply say that they would like to be given the means of finding out whether we are carrying on as we ought to do. I think that in essence the resolution before us to-day is a challenge to the system which prevails and not to the administration of that system.
In my opinion, a parliamentary committee is not the proper body to go into that question. That is a matter of principle which will have to be dealt with upon the introduction of legislation into the house. For several months now-

I will give my own views in that respect. Since May last an interdepartmental committee has been working on the revision of the Customs Act. The committee has met weekly since that time. It consists of the Chairman of the Tariff Board, Judge Sedgewick, Mr. Norman Robertson of the Department of External Affairs; Mr. Hector MacKinnon of the Department of Finance; Mr. H. D. Scully, Commissioner of Customs, and Mr. C. P. Blair, who for a great many years was assistant commissioner of customs. This committee has done a great deal of work on the Customs Act and has advanced the work to this stage, that it is about to circulate its proposals to other departments which are interested in customs administration. When they receive the comments and criticisms of these other departments they will prepare a report on the act and make that report to me, and I shall then introduce the consolidated and revised Customs Act at the next session of parliament. When that legislation is introduced these questions of principle which have been gone into to-day by hon. members will certainly have to be considered at length by the house. I do not know whether the act will be referred to a special committee or to the committee of the whole house, but that will be the time to consider changes in principle and a change in the system if such a change is thought desirable. In view of the fact that the work of revision is under way, I hope that the mover of the resolution will not press it this afternoon.
I think the house is indebted to the hon. member for plunging into the Customs Act and bringing on this discussion. Unfortunately, as the seconder of the resolution said, a great many people fight shy of such a dry subject, and any member of the house who will interest himself in the administration of the act is entitled to credit for so doing. I would suggest, if it is agreeable to the mover of the resolution, that this discussion has served its purpose for the time being; that the resolution be withdrawn, and that this matter be dealt with next year when the Customs Act is before the house.

First of all I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) upon having introduced this resolution, and I hope that this discussion will not close now; for it has not been a discussion. We have heard mly three speakers, the mover and seconder Df the resolution and the minister, and I think it would be regrettable, in view of the fact that legislation will be ;nt'-oduced next session,

if this matter did not receive some consideration from different viewpoints in the house. I hope that the mover will not withdraw the resolution, at least until it has been further
discussed.
I have been interested in public affaire ever since I went to western Canada, nearly thirty years ago-twenty-eight to be exact-and during that time the tariff has been discussed in season and out of season. I came to the conclusion some fifteen years ago, when I was associated with the old Progressive movement, that as far as I could see the tariff had been used more or less as a debating issue or a smoke screen by the two political parties, and that there was in reality very little	difference	in their	administration oftariffs. That impression has been confirmed in the past few years. I have often been taken to task for the statement that the only	difference	I could	see	between thepolicies of the two parties with respect to the tariff was that the Conservatives always advocated a high tariff and that the Liberals when in power maintained a tariff which was high. I could not see the difference between the two. Someone suggests to me, a tariff that was not too	high. I	think	I shall leaveit as	I stated it	originally; for	I think that
is the fact.
The mover of the resolution has performed a service in bringing to the attention of the house the fact that it is not altogether the tariff or the tariff schedule that really counts, but the valuation of goods for duty purposes. The house should go into the matter of valuation for duty purposes much more thoroughly than we have gone into it this afternoon. I was on the farm implements committee last year. The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) referred to some of [DOT]the statements made there, and I recollect how difficult I found it to follow some of the arguments as to the way in which valuations were made for duty purposes.
The mover of the resolution gave certain dates as to when the power of parliament over customs duties had been restricted, if I may put it in that way, by the granting of further power to the minister or to the commissioner of customs. I noted that several of the years he mentioned, 1904, 1907, 1922, 1936, 1937, were all years when we had a Liberal administration in power, and that to a large extent the Liberal party is responsible for the method of valuation and the tariff policies that we now have. And in view of the fact that throughout all these years the tariff has been made an issue in western Canada and throughout Canada-and I say an unreal issue-I would point out to the mover and seconder of the resolution, as well

The Customs Tariff
as to other hon. members, that to-day we have in office a Liberal government with the largest majority which any government has had since confederation, and they should either carry out their declared policy in regard to this matter or drop the discussion altogether.
The other day the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) outlined the history of the matter from the time of confederation, and, if I remember correctly, what he said was to the effect that in a large measure all we have succeeded in doing is dividing the people and creating a lot of hard feeling. That is true. I should like to see the house tackle the economic problems that confront the country. If this government do not intend to do anything in relation to the tariff, then let us tackle some other problems that need to be tackled and cease dividing our people on an issue which apparently is an unreal issue.
Let me add that regulations made by the department often undo the thing that parliament intended to do. I have in mind particularly the $100 exemption which was granted to returning tourists. Regulations have been issued by the department which have negatived that privilege to a very large extent. Last year I spoke of a case of the importation of a set of rubber tires, which could be brought in in the car but could not be brought in on the wheels of the car. This year I was crossing the boundary into Canada and the official asked me if I had anything to declare. As a matter of fact I had not. In the course of conversation with this official he told me of a new regulation which had been put into effect last summer, that if you bring a pair of shoes or an article of clothing bought abroad into the country in your baggage, it comes in free, but if you wear it when you come in it immediately becomes dutiable. Now since most people who cross the border into say the United States and stay forty-eight hours may buy shoes or shirts or some such articles and wear them, is it fair or reasonable or proper that such a person buying something for his own use should pay duty on it, whereas if he brings in something in his baggage, possibly for someone else, it may come in free of duty? I heard an hon. member on the Liberal side say, "Yes, that is fair." I say it is unfair, because it negatives the desire of this parliament to grant that exemption.

radio in the United States and being honest enough to say he had bought the shirt on the former occasion, this made the radio set become dutiable. Now the intention of this parliament in enacting that provision in the 1936 Canada-United States trade agreement, was that it should be given as a privilege to the people of Canada who went abroad on a visit to bring back goods to the value of $100 free of duty.
